assumptions: DEMO DATA: these workloads are synthetic stand-ins whose autocorrelation structure imitates the real traces. The raw traces are 2.5 GB and are not shipped in the container. The *findings* below are the real measured ones.

Open-loop assumption: replaying a trace against a different policy is a counterfactual, valid only because every arrival process here is externally driven and cannot respond to provisioning. Rankings transfer; absolute costs carry a sim-to-real disclaimer.
Simulated numbers are a ceiling by construction. Every simplification in the simulator — the utilisation model, modelled service times, modelled cold starts — flatters the proactive methods.
DELPHI recommends capacity; it never applies a change to anything real.
Retail list prices are not what an enterprise pays. The shape of a frontier is the result, not the absolute dollars.

workloads.label: Synthetic — strong daily rhythm
workloads.licence: Synthetic — generated locally, no external data.
workloads.verdict: Strong daily structure. Forecasting is expected to pay at commitment windows of roughly six hours or longer, where reaction is impossible.

workloads.label: Synthetic — moderate daily rhythm
workloads.licence: Synthetic — generated locally, no external data.
workloads.verdict: Weak daily structure. No forecaster tested beat a trailing percentile at any commitment length on workloads in this range.

workloads.label: Synthetic — weak daily rhythm
workloads.licence: Synthetic — generated locally, no external data.
workloads.verdict: Weak daily structure. No forecaster tested beat a trailing percentile at any commitment length on workloads in this range.

workloads.label: Synthetic — persistent, no rhythm
workloads.licence: Synthetic — generated locally, no external data.
workloads.verdict: Effectively no daily structure. A trailing percentile — or at long horizons a flat average — is the right tool; an explicit forecast only adds its own error.

findings.question: Does forecasting beat reaction at minute-scale autoscaling horizons?
findings.prior: Yes, and the margin should grow with actuation delay.
findings.answer: No. Against a properly tuned sliding-window percentile recommender — the incumbent that Kubernetes VPA and Borg Autopilot already ship — forecasting lost in 8 of 8 settings, and the gap widened with cold start.
findings.evidence: Minute-scale autocorrelation is ~0.98, so a trailing percentile already extracts nearly all the signal; an explicit model adds its own error. Confirmed across four forecasters.

findings.question: Does a price-derived compliance target beat a conventional fixed one?
findings.prior: Only when prices are asymmetric enough to matter.
findings.answer: Yes in 19 of 24 settings. The newsvendor identity q* = C_u/(C_u+C_o) sets the percentile that convention normally fixes at p95.
findings.evidence: At C_u/C_o = 19 the derived target equals the p95 convention exactly and the two agree to the cent — a forced algebraic identity that serves as a consistency check on the harness.

findings.question: Is there a workload where no controller beats static provisioning?
findings.answer: Yes. On a stable Azure Functions workload, static provisioning was the cheapest point on the entire frontier and neither calibrated controller reached a 1% violation rate at all.
findings.evidence: Demand p95/mean was near 1.2; there was nothing for a forecaster to add.

findings.question: Does forecasting ever pay, and if so where?
findings.prior: Unknown after Q1 refuted the autoscaling case.
findings.answer: Yes, in the commitment regime: sizing once and holding for 6-12 hours on a workload with strong daily structure. Forward forecasting dominated a trailing window — cheaper AND fewer violations — in 5 of 7 and 6 of 7 quantile settings, halving the violation rate at lower cost at 12 hours.
findings.evidence: Two conditions are both necessary: daily autocorrelation above ~0.5, and a commitment long enough that reaction is impossible. Either alone is not enough.

findings.question: Does week-ahead forecasting work?
findings.prior: Seasonality should dominate at long horizons.
findings.answer: No. On the only fleet long enough to test it (13 weeks), a flat average of the prior four weeks beat every structured predictor: 53.1% error versus 56-60%.
findings.evidence: Weekly autocorrelation was 0.271 against a daily 0.248 — both weak. There was no long-range structure to exploit.

findings.question: Does daily autocorrelation predict whether forecasting will pay?
findings.prior: Proposed as a diagnostic after the mixed results above.
findings.answer: It predicted every outcome measured so far. High-autocorrelation workloads reward forecasting at long commitments; low-autocorrelation ones never did, at any commitment length.
findings.evidence: Across 7 workloads x 4 forecasters x 4 quantiles, the 0.50 cutoff gets 27 of 28 cells right at a 6-hour commitment. But there is a real exception in the unflattering direction: materna-2 at r=0.450, below the threshold, won 2 of 4 at 12 hours while materna-1 at r=0.494, above it, won none. Autocorrelation orders these workloads well and predicts the extremes reliably; it is not a calibrated boundary, and a value near 0.45-0.50 does not settle the question.
